paras: The Sycamore station lynching threat was a gathering of about 300 people at Sycamore station, in Pittsylvania County, Virginia, on February 6, 1882, who meant to lynch W. H. Yeatts, a prisoner accused of murdering a local merchant there four days earlier. Warned of the crowd, officers at Lynchburg held Yeatts back and that evening sent him to the county jail at Chatham on a train that did not stop at Sycamore. The Associated Press carried the story nationally as a murderer's narrow escape, and Yeatts was later tried, convicted and hanged at Chatham in August 1882.

According to a Lynchburg telegram, Atkinson, a merchant at Sycamore on the Virginia Midland railroad, was found shot through the head near his store on February 3, and a man named Yates, last seen with him, had disappeared. The Richmond Dispatch identified the man as W. H. Yeatts, "commonly called Ham. Yeatts," a former Lynchburg tobacco merchant who had married the night before the killing, and the Lynchburg News said he was believed to have killed Atkinson for robbery. Traced by Lynchburg police, Yeatts was arrested at Bristol early on Saturday, February 4, and brought back to Lynchburg the next day by Officer Gouldman.

On February 6 officers prepared to take Yeatts from Lynchburg to the county jail at Chatham. According to the Associated Press, they learned that "a crowd of about 300 people had congregated at Sycamore station, the scene of the murder, with the determination of lynching the prisoner." A special dispatch to the Washington National Republican added that the Pittsylvania sheriff "refused to receive tho prisoner owing to tho excited crowd" waiting at Sycamore.

The Evening Critic's later account said that passengers on a northbound train brought news to the Lynchburg depot of preparations and threats, so the guards, Sergeant Irvine and Sheriff Overby, returned the prisoner to the Lynchburg jail. That evening, after the crowd had dispersed by the Critic's account, he was sent through on the fast mail, which made no stop at Sycamore, and no violence is reported.

At Chatham, Yeatts was chained to the floor of his cell, and the Critic wrote that "so frequent woro tho tumors of violence, that an extra guard was placed nreund tho Jail." No report of an arrest of anyone in the Sycamore crowd appears in the coverage. In May a jury at Chatham found him guilty of first-degree murder of Presley E. Adkerson, as the victim was named in later reports, and he was sentenced to hang on July 27.

After Governor Cameron granted a one-week respite, a Chatham dispatch reported that 75 to 100 men came to the jail before dawn one Saturday to take Yeatts and hang him, believing his sentence commuted. They dispersed when Adkerson's stepfather told them he had only been respited, and Yeatts was hanged at Chatham in early August.

The Associated Press item, datelined Lynchburg, February 6, ran the next day in the Savannah Morning News, the Washington Evening Star, the Wheeling Intelligencer and the Richmond Dispatch. Headlines presented it as a near miss for the prisoner: "Vengeance Threatened" in Savannah, "A Murderer Saved from Lynching" in the Evening Star, "A Narrow Escape" in Wheeling. The Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman headed it "Judge Lynch Intercepted," and the Bismarck Tribune "Escaped Lynching."

Every version called Yeatts "the murderer" before any trial, spelling his name Yates, Yeates or "Yester." None criticized the crowd; the Richmond Dispatch printed the wire item beneath its own accounts of "the foul crime" and the effort to bring "the assassin to justice." At the execution, the Dispatch recalled in one clause that "the excited citizens of the neighborhood had made threats and some preparations to lynch the murderer." No article states the race of Yeatts, his victim or the crowd; the Critic described both men as from families of "the highest respectability."

The Bristol News and the Lynchburg News placed the arrest on February 4, the Dispatch's August retrospective on February 5; the Bristol paper credited Sergeant D. A. Wheeler with it, while the Critic said Gouldman made it. The wire said officers had started for Chatham before turning back, whereas the Critic placed the warning at the Lynchburg depot.

bases: A crowd of about 300 gathered at Sycamore station intending to lynch a prisoner accused of murder, and officers kept him away from it (A2, A7, A17).

A crowd of about 300 meant to lynch Yeatts for an alleged murder, but officers sent him past Sycamore on a train that did not stop and he was not harmed (A2, A17); he was later hanged legally after trial (A16, A17).

The AP wire (A2, A4), a separate special dispatch to the National Republican (A7) and the later Dispatch and Evening Critic retrospectives (A16, A17) agree that a crowd at Sycamore threatened to lynch the prisoner and that officers kept him from it.

accounts.label: Associated Press, Lynchburg
accounts.gist: Officers started for Chatham with the prisoner but, learning that about 300 people had gathered at Sycamore station to lynch him, brought him back and sent him that evening on the fast mail, which made no stop at Sycamore.

accounts.label: Special Lynchburg dispatch
accounts.gist: The Pittsylvania sheriff arrived but refused to receive the prisoner owing to the excited crowd awaiting him at Sycamore.

accounts.label: Evening Critic execution story
accounts.gist: News from passengers on a northbound train of preparations and threats reached the Lynchburg depot, so the guards returned him to jail and took him through at night, after the crowd had dispersed, on a train that did not stop at the station.

framing.detail: The AP item ran under headlines such as 'Vengeance Threatened', 'A Murderer Saved from Lynching', 'A Narrow Escape' and 'Judge Lynch Intercepted', each calling the untried prisoner 'the murderer'.
The Richmond Dispatch framed the case around 'the foul crime' and bringing 'the assassin to justice', appending the wire item on the crowd without comment.
Execution stories recalled the threats in a clause as a sign of local excitement over the murder.

conflicts.note: The contemporary Bristol and Lynchburg reports put the arrest on Saturday; the August retrospective says the 5th.
